native_result.query: In the PCA on the forms of capital analyzed in hundred-year time slices, during the Younger Bronze Age (1100-500 BCE), how does the principal component value of PC1 in the beginning of the period at 1100 BCE differ from the subsequent time horizons between 1000 to 500 BCE?
native_result.HypoA: The beginning of the Younger Bronze Age (1100 BCE) is associated with negative values on the first principal component (PC1), while the majority of time horizons (1000-500 BCE) are characterized by positive values on PC1. This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: PC1 of the forms of capital peaks at 1100 BCE (+4.45) and is lower in every subsequent Younger Bronze Age horizon: PC1 = 4.452 (1100 BCE), 2.172 (1000), 1.654 (900), 1.910 (800), 1.247 (700), 0.829 (600), 0.815 (500 BCE), giving six positive differences score(1100)-score(bin) of +2.280, +2.798, +2.542, +3.205, +3.623 and +3.636. The trajectory is a step-drop followed by a non-monotonic plateau with its minimum at 500 BCE, not a monotonic decline: a large immediate drop at 1000 BCE, then a low plateau of ~0.8-2.2 with a slight mid-window dip at 900 BCE and a partial rebound at 800 BCE (800 lies above 900), and the lowest values at 600-500 BCE. We therefore hypothesize that the beginning of the Younger Bronze Age was a brief maximum in overall capital accumulation and elaboration, after which capital investment fell steeply and stabilized at a low level that drifted slightly lower to its minimum at 500 BCE. The 1100 BCE excess is driven by social capital - copper/gold (ZCU_AU, +0.90 to +1.30 per contrast) and monument count (ZMonument, +0.36) - and by symbolic capital, house size (Zhausgr, +0.45 to +0.50) and dagger (ZDolch, +0.41 to +0.46), with economic capital contributing via deposits (ZHort, +0.57 to +1.25 against 900-500 BCE); cultural capital is the only negative term (-0.21), because pottery decoration rises after 1100 BCE while pottery form is unchanged. Crucially, what collapses immediately at 1000 BCE is copper-gold, house size and dagger, not deposits: ZHort stays at 3.38 at both 1100 and 1000 BCE, so the economic gap opens only from 900 BCE and widens from 700 BCE - the 1100 BCE peak is thus a metal/house/monument maximum with a one-century-long hoard-deposition tail. The pattern is not an artifact of carried-forward data (constant columns ZSichel, ZKeform and near-constant ZAxtSchwert, Zamber, ZBeil contribute -0.06 to +0.02, while all named drivers vary with sd 0.6-1.6 inside the window), it survives exact mean-0/sd-1 re-standardization (all six signs identical, bin ordering identical), and although PC1 explains only 31.8% of variance, PC2 independently marks 1100 BCE as the sole positive-score bin in the window, i.e. 1100 BCE is an outlier in the full capital space.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection (decimal=',' parsing; grid, missingness, standardization, cross-check against time_series_data.csv). 2) PCA via SVD on the mean-centred 39x12 Z matrix (all 39 rows, Z as supplied); PC1 oriented once to a positive loading sum (raw SVD sign reported, no per-slice refit/refip); PC1/PC2 scores read at the 7 YBA rows. 3) Signed differences score(1100)-score(bin) decomposed per variable as loading_v*(x_v,1100-x_v,bin), aggregated to symbolic/social/cultural/economic forms; contributions verified to sum exactly to each difference. 4) Carry-forward kill-list from within-YBA sd (threshold 0.15). 5) Robustness: exact mean0/sd1 re-standardization over 39 rows -> signs, magnitudes, bin ordering (cos 0.996, Spearman 1.000). 6) Belau pollen PC1 aligned for 1100-800 BCE only, labelled interpretation, excluded from the headline claim. 7) Final revision (this turn, no re-run): score table restated in strict chronological order and 'monotonic decline' corrected to step-drop + non-monotonic plateau with minimum at 500 BCE; depot-step caveat retained, so the 1000 BCE drop is attributed to copper-gold, house size and dagger rather than deposits.
